candidates.text:
Let
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
For every \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus \(f_n\to f\) pointwise. If \((f_n)\) converged uniformly, its uniform limit would necessarily be this pointwise limit \(f\).

Take \(\varepsilon=\tfrac14\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), set \(n=N\) and \(x_N=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x_N<1\), so \(f(x_N)=0\), whereas
\[
f_N(x_N)=\left(2^{-1/N}\right)^N=\frac12.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|f_N(x_N)-f(x_N)|=\frac12>\varepsilon.
\]
Hence no \(N\) satisfies the definition of uniform convergence, and therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).

For each \(x\in[0,1)\), we have \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus the pointwise limit is
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Fix \(\varepsilon_0=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), take \(n=N\) and \(x_N=2^{-1/N}\in[0,1)\). Then \(f(x_N)=0\) and
\[
|f_N(x_N)-f(x_N)|=x_N^N=\tfrac12.
\]
Hence, for every \(N\), there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) for which \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon_0\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).

For each \(x\in[0,1)\), we have \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Take \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), set \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x\in[0,1)\), so \(f(x)=0\), whereas
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Hence, for every \(N\), there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly to its pointwise limit. Since any uniform limit must also be the pointwise limit, the sequence does not converge uniformly to any function on \([0,1]\).

problem.theorem: Define $f_{n}:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_{n}(x)=x^{n}$. Show that the sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)$ does not converge uniformly.
